```{r}
#| eval:  false
#| echo: false
words <- c("church", "gay", "sex", "marriage", "cheat")
pattern <- str_c(r"(\b)", str_c(words, collapse = r"(\b|\b)"), r"(\b)")
pattern 
pudding |>
  # Extract ALL matching words from each row as a list
  mutate(match = str_extract_all(question_only, regex(pattern, ignore_case = TRUE))) |>
  # Expand list elements into individual rows
  unnest(match) |>
  # Convert to lowercase so "Hello" and "hello" count together
  mutate(match = str_to_lower(match)) |>
  # Count occurrences per word
  count(match, name = "count")

match
```


```{r}
#| eval:  false
#| echo: false
# Install and load packages
install.packages(c("ggplot2", "ggwordcloud", "dplyr", "tidytext"))
library(ggplot2)
library(ggwordcloud)
library(dplyr)
library(tidytext)

# Sample text data processing using tidytext
text_data <- tibble(text = c("R is great for data science.", 
                             "Word clouds visualize word frequencies in text data.",
                             "ggplot2 and ggwordcloud make beautiful plots in R."))

# Tokenize and count frequencies
words_df <- text_data %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, text) %>%
  anti_join(stop_words) %>%
  count(word, sort = TRUE)

# Generate Word Cloud
set.seed(42) # For reproducible placement
ggplot(words_df, aes(label = word, size = n, color = n)) +
  geom_text_wordcloud() +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 20) + # Controls maximum font size
  scale_color_gradient(low = "skyblue", high = "darkblue") +
  theme_minimal()
```


```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: false
library(wordcloud2)

# Input requires a 2-column data frame (word, freq)
df <- data.frame(
  word = c("R", "Data", "Science", "Visualization", "Ggplot", "Code", "Analysis"),
  freq = c(50, 40, 35, 30, 25, 20, 15)
)

# Render interactive HTML cloud
wordcloud2(data = df, size = 0.7, shape = 'circle', color = 'random-dark')
```


# Where do you get intimate advice?

Seeking advice from friends is not always easy. Not everyone is a good confidant and sometimes our secrets are too embarrasing or too delicate to reveal outloud. For centuries, the truthwordy confidants of people with power were individuals bound by a vow of secrecy, priest for example.  With the development of the printed press and later the radio, people found a chance to anonimously shared their stories and ask for advice. 

In Spain the most famous radio advice show, *El Consultorio de Elena Francis*, run continuously from 1947 to 1984. For nearly four decades, millions of Spanish women tuned in or wrote letters to *Señora Francis* seeking guidance on personal issues, relationship struggles, family drama, and domestic problems. Interestingly, the show became the moral watchdog of the Franco regime.  The responses broadcasted reflected the conservative, patriarchal, and Catholic values endorsed by the Francoist regime. Advice frequently encouraged women to endure infidelity, domestic hardship, or mistreatment, emphasizing patience, devotion, and submission to preserve the family structure.  

The *Señora Francis* of the USA is *Dear Abby*, a column that has been runnng countiously since 1956 and has been sindycated in more than 1,200 newspapers. The letters sent to Dear Abby have been compilated by **The Pudding**, an award-winning digital publication that creates visual essays and interactive data visualizations to explain culturally debated topics and complex ideas. 

In the The Putting article, [30 Years of American Anxietis](https://pudding.cool/2018/11/dearabby/#histogram__category--religion), authors Ilia Blinderman, Caitlyn Ralph, and Russell Samora (with illustrations by Thoka Maer) identify *the most debated topics* by Dear Abby readers:  sex, religion, and LGBTQ issues. The articule include =s some of the letters that are worth reading. 

Here, I do my own analysis of `r total_letters` *Dear Abby* letters from 1985 to 2017 from an archive which can be found in the [The Pudding Github site](https://github.com/the-pudding/data/tree/master/dearabby). 

I am using **word clouds** to reveal some of the most prevalent topics of the letters. No filters were applied to the top cloud including all the available letters (1985-2017), so words like abby appear, as expected, with high frequency. For the clouds for specific years, I have removed a list of words including Abby, dear, advice, letter, and letters.



```{r}
#| echo: false
# 1. Tokenize, remove standard stop words, and count frequencies
words_df <- pudding %>%
  select(question_only) %>%
  drop_na(question_only) %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, question_only) %>%
  anti_join(stop_words, by = "word") %>%
  # Filter out numbers or non-alphabetical tokens if desired
  filter(str_detect(word, "^[a-z]+$")) %>%
  count(word, sort = TRUE) %>%
  # Keep top 100 most frequent words for readability
  slice_max(n, n = 100)

# 2. Generate the Word Cloud
set.seed(42) # Ensures consistent word placement across runs
ggplot(words_df, aes(label = word, size = n, color = n)) +
  geom_text_wordcloud(grid_size = 1, max_grid_size = 32) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 15) +
  scale_color_gradient(low = "skyblue3", high = "midnightblue") +
  theme_minimal()

#The code above was generated by Google Gemini. 
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
# Define your custom words to ignore
custom_stops <- tibble(word = c("abby", "ago", "advice", "dear", "letter", "letters"))
```

# Year 1985
```{r}
#| echo: false
# 1. Tokenize, remove standard stop words, and count frequencies
words_df <- pudding %>%
  filter(year == 1985) %>%
  select(question_only) %>%
  drop_na(question_only) %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, question_only) %>%
  anti_join(stop_words, by = "word") %>%
  anti_join(custom_stops, by = "word") %>%    # Removes YOUR custom words
  # Filter out numbers or non-alphabetical tokens if desired
  filter(str_detect(word, "^[a-z]+$")) %>%
  count(word, sort = TRUE) %>%
  # Keep top 100 most frequent words for readability
  slice_max(n, n = 50)

# 3. Generate the Word Cloud
set.seed(42) # Ensures consistent word placement across runs
ggplot(words_df, aes(label = word, size = n, color = n)) +
  geom_text_wordcloud(grid_size = 1, max_grid_size = 32) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 15) +
  scale_color_gradient(low = "orange", high = "red") +
  theme_minimal()

#The code above was generated by Google Gemini. 
```

# Husband in 1985
```{r}
#| echo: false
# 1. Filter rows containing "husband", tokenize, remove stop words, and count frequencies
words_df <- pudding %>%
  filter(year == 1985) %>%
  select(question_only) %>%
  drop_na(question_only) %>%
  # KEEP ONLY ROWS CONTAINING "husband"
  filter(str_detect(question_only, "husband")) %>% 
  unnest_tokens(word, question_only) %>%
  anti_join(stop_words, by = "word") %>%
  anti_join(custom_stops, by = "word") %>%    # Removes YOUR custom words
  # Filter out numbers or non-alphabetical tokens if desired
  filter(str_detect(word, "^[a-z]+$")) %>%
 # REMOVE THE WORD "husband" FROM THE WORD LIST ITSELF
  filter(word != "husband") %>%
  count(word, sort = TRUE) %>%
  # Keep top 50 most frequent words for readability
  slice_max(n, n = 80)

# 2. Generate the Word Cloud
set.seed(42) # Ensures consistent word placement across runs
ggplot(words_df, aes(label = word, size = n, color = n)) +
  geom_text_wordcloud(grid_size = 1, max_grid_size = 32) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 15) +
  scale_color_gradient(low = "orange", high = "red") +
  theme_minimal()

```
